author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Amplitude: keeping separate instrument tracks playing
summary: Harmonix’s rhythm game for PS2 combines three musical-note buttons with changes between instrument lanes. Keeping the song playing requires both timing and attention.
heroAlt: A real mixing console illustrating separate audio channels; not an Amplitude screenshot or a photograph of its production studio

blocks.text: Harmonix released Amplitude for PS2 in 2003. The player moved between lanes representing instruments and completed note patterns with three note buttons. Successfully completing a phrase kept that instrument playing while the player moved to another lane. The challenge combined accurate button timing with decisions about which musical part needed attention next.
Separate input of musical notes from lane selection

The note buttons controlled the current pattern, while lateral movement selected another instrument lane. This separated performing a phrase from choosing where to play next. Several musical parts could therefore create a complex task with relatively few controls. The DualShock controller supported both decisions without requiring a separate physical instrument for each sound.
Use separate recordings of the instruments

Harmonix’s retrospective explains that artists and labels supplied separate instrument recordings, often called stems. These recordings let the game control individual musical parts while preserving the original performances. A single stereo mix would not offer the same clean separation. Obtaining suitable audio material was therefore an essential part of making the design work.
Make approaching musical notes easier to read

The developers describe Amplitude’s relationship to FreQuency, including changes to its visual presentation and game engine. The display had to help players recognize approaching musical-note patterns and select the next instrument. These choices affected play directly: attractive graphics alone would not help if players could not understand the music and controls in time.
Preserve timing together with the image

When emulating a rhythm game, audio continuity and input timing matter alongside image quality. The correspondence between displayed notes and the soundtrack is central to Amplitude’s design. This is an observation about the game, not a measured emulator comparison. The original PS2 release is also distinct from the later Amplitude reboot and its different implementation.
